title: On handling free variables in interior-point methods for conic linear optimization
contribution: A regularization strategy for free variables in infeasible primal-dual IPMs, with a δ-update rule backed by a global convergence proof and an SDPT3 implementation that matches or beats splitting, quadratic-cone and indefinite-system approaches in accuracy.
problem_entry: Free variables make the Newton system indefinite, so Cholesky cannot be used; splitting loses interior and boundedness; Mészáros's LP regularization had only an ad hoc δ update without convergence theory (pp. 2-3, 9).
key_idea: View the regularized direction as an inexact Newton step and accept it only if δ‖Δz‖ ≤ βσμ/2, halving δ otherwise; keep the Kojima-Megiddo-Mizuno framework (Algorithm 2, pp. 9-10).
assumptions: Analysis in LP form (SOCP/SDP asserted as well known); A full row rank, E full column rank, interior feasibility, initial r_p = r_d1 = 0 for brevity (pp. 4, 6); experiments deliberately violate full column rank of E (p. 12).
proof_devices: repair of one proposition: inexactness breaks r_α = (1-α)r, and the bound δ‖Δz‖ ≤ βσμ/2 restores the neighbourhood inequality with α* halved (Proposition 5.2, p. 11)
global convergence by a uniform positive step-size lower bound α* on a compact set (Theorem 3.1 proof, p. 7; Theorem 5.1, p. 10)
experiments: SDPT3 3.02, four free-variable treatments, 135 instances (DIMACS, modified SDPLIB with full and half rank E, quantum chemistry, moment relaxations); log10 of max DIMACS error; regularization equal or clearly better in accuracy, more iterations, less time per iteration (pp. 12-14).
positioning: Revisits Mészáros (LP) and extends Kojima-Megiddo-Mizuno; chooses a convergent but non-polynomial scheme over inexact-IPM theory (Freund-Jarre-Mizuno, Zhou-Toh) because the latter was harder to implement and worked worse in their tests (pp. 8-9).
writing: Explicit 'Some remarks' section stating what is not claimed and why SDPT3 was chosen (p. 3); closes with three criteria for a good regularization strategy (p. 9).
limits_future: Not claimed best in all situations; only SDPT3 tested; SeDuMi already handles split variables well; no polynomial bound; open: regularization inside SeDuMi and an easy polynomial update rule (pp. 3-4, 14).

method_links.note: Simple variant chosen because it works in code; an implemented theoretical alternative reported as worse; the failed nonincreasing-δ design recorded with its reason.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Inexactness budget tied to the duality gap
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Cheap regularized step admitted by bounding its error by the centring term βσμ/2, which lets a classical convergence proof go through with one proposition repaired.

transferable: Find the single inequality of a classical convergence proof that an approximate step breaks, and add an acceptance test (with a shrink loop) that restores it (p. 10).
Allow a control parameter to increase again from a best current guess rather than forcing monotonicity, and report the monotone design that failed (p. 11).
Compare methods with different stopping behaviour by the best log10 DIMACS error reached during the run (p. 13).

quotes.text: We emphasize that free variables are a computational issue and not a theoretical one.
Ultimately, we believe that our analysis allows us to identify the essence of a good regularization strategy. It should (i) be convergent, (ii) be easy to implement, and (iii) work well in practice.

title: SDPLR 1.03-beta User's Guide (short version)
contribution: Installation, usage and input-format documentation for the SDPLR low-rank SDP solver, including a low-rank extension of the sparse SDPA format.
problem_entry: Software documentation for a C package for large-scale SDP with source, binaries and a Matlab interface (p. 1).
key_idea: Input format extends sparse SDPA with low-rank data blocks given as BDB^T; a reserved line will carry the primal trace for ±1 combinatorial SDPs to give dual bounds during the run (pp. 3-4).
assumptions: n/a (software); build needs BLAS/LAPACK and the bundled GSL (pp. 1-2).
positioning: Lists Burer, Monteiro and Choi as developers (p. 1); builds on the community SDPA format (p. 3).
writing: Terse step-by-step guide; worked example is the Lovász theta SDP of the 5-cycle (pp. 4-5).
limits_future: Dual-bound feature for ±1 SDPs announced as in development (p. 4).

method_links.note: The low-rank prototype of 2000 is maintained as public software with Matlab and command-line entry points.
Weak: the input format exposes low-rank structure of the data, the same structure the factorization method exploits.

transferable: Ship a solver with a structure-aware input format defined as a small extension of the community standard, with a classic toy instance (theta of C5) as the format example (pp. 3-5).
Provide an interactive parameter-file generator with inline explanations (p. 3).
coauthors: Renato D. C. Monteiro, Changhui Choi

quotes.text: SDPLR is a C software package for solving large-scale semidefinite programming problems.
The SDPLR format, which SDPLR is also capable of handling, is more or less an extension of sparse SDPA format which also allows low-rank data matrices to be specified easily.

title: The difference between 5×5 doubly nonnegative and completely positive matrices
contribution: Shows that every 5×5 DNN-but-not-CP matrix is a CP matrix plus a single extremely bad (rank-3 cyclic extreme) matrix, gives a finite CP-reduction procedure, and a sharp copositive cut separating extremely bad matrices from C5.
problem_entry: D_n = C_n only for n ≤ 4, so n = 5 is the first gap; from optimization, C_n is the true domain and D_n only a tractable approximation (p. 3).
key_idea: Parameterize extremely bad matrices as ΛRR^TΛ under 12 permutation classes, peel off rank-one CP pieces by LPs until irreducible, prove irreducible ⇔ extremely bad for n = 5, then separate with a scaled, permuted Horn matrix (pp. 4-13).
assumptions: n ≥ 5 generally, n = 5 for the main results; extreme-ray characterization of D5 taken from Hamilton-Jester and Li (pp. 3-4).
proof_devices: range-condition characterization of CP-reducibility (Theorem 4, p. 7)
potential rank + nonzero count strictly decreasing for finiteness (Theorem 5, pp. 8-9)
case analysis over permutation classes with scaling invariance (Lemma 3, Theorems 6-7, pp. 9-12)
Farkas alternatives for two index sets reduced to sign contradictions (pp. 11-12)
Horn-matrix cut K = P Diag(w) H Diag(w) P^T with w = -(P^T X P ∘ H)^{-1} e (Lemma 4, Theorem 8, pp. 12-13)
experiments: none; worked examples (Algorithm 1 iteration, p. 8; 5-cycle stable set where one cut closes the ϑ' gap, pp. 13-14).
positioning: Builds on Burer 2009 copositive representation and on Berman-Xu, Xu, Johnson-Reams; notes their cut coincides with Bomze-Locatelli-Tardella's inequality derived differently (pp. 2-3, 14).
writing: Coins 'bad' and 'extremely bad' matrices to keep the optimization perspective in view (p. 3); states the open problem plainly (pp. 12-13).
limits_future: No separation for an arbitrary bad matrix (open, tied to an outer description of C5); Algorithm 1 is not polynomial and need not recover a CP factorization of CP input (pp. 8-9, 12-13).

method_links.note: After packaging QP in the CP cone, the follow-up attacks that cone: its gap to the DNN approximation and a separating cut.
Works in the smallest dimension where the question is nontrivial (n = 5), gives an explicit description, and publishes the boundary as an open problem.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Decompose the relaxation's excess into good part plus one irreducible bad piece
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Every point of D5 \ C5 is CP plus a single extremely bad matrix, which is then cut off.

transferable: Study the extreme rays of the tractable cone that lie outside the target cone, parameterize them explicitly, and show every point of the gap is target-cone plus one such ray (pp. 4-6, 12).
Prove finiteness of a peeling algorithm with a potential such as rank plus nonzero count that must drop at each line-search stop (pp. 8-9).
Test a new cut on the canonical gap instance (stable set on C5) and relate it to cuts derived elsewhere (p. 14).

quotes.text: This terminology reinforces the perspective from optimization applications involving CP matrices [5], where Cn is the true domain of interest and Dn serves only as a (tractable) approximation of Cn.
We have not been able to derive a separating inequality for an arbitrary bad matrix, but we show below how to separate an extremely bad matrix

title: A p-cone sequential relaxation procedure for 0-1 integer programs
contribution: A family of p-order-cone lift-and-project operators for 0-1 programs that contains Lovász-Schrijver (p = ∞) and Balas-Ceria-Cornuéjols (|J| = 1) as special cases, converges asymptotically to the integer hull, has the lowest iteration complexity at p = 2, but loses to the LP version in computation.
problem_entry: All prior sequential lift-and-project procedures use LP or SDP in the lifted space; ask whether p-order-cone programming yields procedures with their own advantages (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Multiply each linear constraint by the p-ball constraint circumscribing {0,1}^J, linearize X = xx^T keeping only diag(X) = x, and project (pp. 5-6).
assumptions: P ⊆ [0,1]^n compact convex, possibly semi-infinite; symmetry and PSD of X deliberately not imposed for the theory; complexity result for polytopes (pp. 5, 8, 14).
proof_devices: monotonicity in the set and in p via a convexity lemma (Propositions 3.7, 3.9, Lemma 3.8, pp. 15-16)
barrier-parameter iteration bounds O(√|I|) at p = 2 (Corollary 3.6, p. 14)

escalating geometry: polytope (two proofs), then ball via n nearly-active perturbed constraints, Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury and θ → 0 Taylor expansion, then general convex set via a supporting ball (pp. 16-20)
asymptotic convergence by contradiction and a continuity argument (Theorem 4.1, pp. 21-22)
explicit polytope family P(a) requiring infinitely many rounds (Proposition 4.2, pp. 22-23)
experiments: p = 2 (MOSEK 5.0) vs p = ∞ (CPLEX 9.0 dual simplex, MOSEK IPM) on 8 DIMACS stable-set graphs and 7 small MIPLIB 2003 instances; the LP is faster with better bounds, refuting the stated hypothesis (pp. 23-25).
positioning: Unifies Lovász-Schrijver, Balas-Ceria-Cornuéjols and relates to Kojima-Tunçel (whose asymptotic proof needs all rank-2 products, unlike theirs); distinguishes from Kim-Kojima SOCP relaxations derived from semidefiniteness (pp. 9-11, 21, 26).
writing: States the computational hypothesis before the negative result ('We had hypothesized'); closes by calling the contribution theoretical with possible future computational gains (pp. 23, 25-26).
limits_future: No finite convergence and no rate; SOCP not competitive; hope for better SOCP software (pp. 21-23, 25-26).

method_links.note: Lift then one parameterized cone family that contains the classical procedures as special cases (unification), rather than an exact reformulation.
Order reversed: theory carries the paper and computation, run afterwards, refutes the computational hypothesis; printed openly (consistent with H8).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Escalating-geometry proof (polytope → ball → general convex set)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Cut-off of fractional extreme points proved for polytopes, extended to balls by perturbed nearly-active constraints, then to any compact convex set through a supporting ball and monotonicity.

transferable: Generate a relaxation family by multiplying valid linear constraints by a norm-ball constraint circumscribing the 0-1 points; the norm p becomes a monotone strength/complexity dial (pp. 5, 14-16).
Justify a new operator by showing classical operators are parameter settings of it (pp. 9-11).
Extend a polytope argument to general convex sets by enclosing P in a ball that supports it at the extreme point, then apply monotonicity (pp. 18-20).
State the computational hypothesis before the experiment so a negative result reads as a test (p. 23).

quotes.text: Our hope is that, by introducing POCP relaxations, we might discover new lift-and-project procedures that have their own theoretical and computational advantages.
These results are a testament to the high quality of current LP software.

title: Relaxing the optimality conditions of box QP
contribution: SDP relaxations of box QP that encode first- and second-order necessary conditions via an index-free reformulation; they equal Shor's bounded relaxation at the root but reduce B&B nodes on subboxes, plus a fractional-times-longest-edge branching rule.
problem_entry: Global box QP needs strong cheap relaxations; first-order KKT had been used before; the second-order condition depends on the unknown inactive set (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: With w = x∘(e-x), local convexity Q_II ⪰ 0 becomes Q∘ww^T ⪰ 0; relax it, with complementarity, in one lifted PSD matrix (SDP12) or a lean version (SDP2) (pp. 4-7).
assumptions: Q indefinite; bounded Shor relaxation with diag(X) ≤ x, since without it the SDP is unbounded (pp. 1, 5).
proof_devices: extend-an-optimum lemma for equal optimal values (Lemma 4.1, p. 7)
dual complementary slackness gives Q_JJ ⪰ 0 on J = {X_ii < x_i} (Lemma 4.2, p. 8)
feasible paths and directional derivatives show SDP0 optima satisfy first-order inequalities (Propositions 4.4-4.6, Theorem 4.8, pp. 9-11)
explicit lifted point with large constant via Schur complement and null-space lemma (pp. 11-13)
experiments: B&B in MATLAB/YALMIP/SeDuMi, 100 random n = 20 instances; advanced branching −44% nodes and time; SDP2 −21% nodes but more CPU; switching scheme partly successful; SDP12 −65% nodes, slowest (pp. 15-20).
positioning: Extends Vandenbussche-Nemhauser and Burer-Vandenbussche (first-order) to second-order; contrasts with Nesterov's smooth p-norm boxes (p. 2).
writing: Announces the main theorem as 'surprising, somewhat negative' up front and pairs it with a positive B&B finding (p. 2); disclaims building a best B&B (p. 13).
limits_future: Root equivalence; CPU loss; only small random instances; future: QP over the simplex, faster SDP software (pp. 18-20).

method_links.note: Strengthen Shor with more valid structure and test whether it goes strictly beyond; at the root it does not (equivalence), gains appear only on subdivided boxes.
Testbed is 100 unfiltered uniform random instances, before his later engineered hard pools.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Relax the optimality conditions, not only the feasible set
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Second-order condition written index-free and lifted into the SDP; continues first-order KKT relaxations and is proposed for other QP classes.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Root-equivalent relaxations can differ inside B&B
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: SDP0 = SDP2 = SDP12 in value at the root, yet SDP2/SDP12 cut nodes on subboxes.

transferable: Encode a condition that depends on an unknown active set through a weight vector vanishing exactly on active indices (w = x∘(e-x)), giving one matrix inequality (pp. 4-5).
Prove equivalence of a strengthened relaxation by constructing a feasible point of it from an optimum of the weak one, filling extra blocks via a Schur complement with a large scalar (pp. 11-13).
Branch at the relaxation's solution coordinate weighted by edge length, since SDP enforces X = xx^T weakly in the interior (p. 16).
Show B&B comparisons as per-instance log-log scatter plots against y = x (pp. 17-19).

quotes.text: In Sect. 4, we prove the surprising, somewhat negative result that all three achieve the same optimal value.

Relaxing the standard second-order necessary optimality conditions is one of the main theoretical ideas of this paper. This task is non-trivial since it implicitly involves knowledge of the active/inactive constraint set at a general point.

title: A semidefinite programming approach to the hypergraph minimum bisection problem
contribution: The first exact mathematical program (a QCQP) for hypergraph minimum bisection via its complement, an SDP relaxation solved by SDPLR with tight bounds and METIS-competitive rounded solutions on circuit benchmarks, and partial results towards an approximation guarantee.
problem_entry: HMB is NP-hard and served by heuristics, with no known equivalent mathematical program; work on the complement because only it has approximation results in the graph case (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Ternary hyperedge indicators y_i with y_i^2 - y_i x_j = 0 for j in E_i make max Σ w_i y_i^2 count uncut edges exactly; lift to an SDP and round with balanced Goemans-Williamson plus FM local search (pp. 4-5, 9).
proof_devices: Gram-vector geometry: vertices of a hyperedge lie on a disc around the hyperedge vector (Proposition 4.1, Corollary 4.2, pp. 10-11)
Lagrangian stationary-point lemma for a hyperplane missing a disc (Lemma 4.3, pp. 11-12)
uncut-probability lower bound (Proposition 4.4, p. 13) shown to vanish as O((n+m)^-2) by an F-distribution and one-tailed Chebyshev argument (Proposition 4.6, pp. 14-15)
experiments: 15 ISPD98 circuits, SDPLR 1.02 with loosened tolerance, against best of 100 METIS runs; mean SDP gap 1.97% (max 7.99%); competitive cuts at 45-55% balance; much slower (12 h vs 6 s on the largest) (pp. 7-9).
positioning: Follows Goemans-Williamson, Ye-Zhang (0.602 for graph bisection complement) and Choi-Ye clique expansion; contrasts with METIS heuristics (pp. 3, 6).
writing: Section titled 'Towards an approximation guarantee'; explicitly calls the theory 'somewhat disappointing' relative to computation (pp. 9, 15).
limits_future: No approximation guarantee; tighter relaxation and faster SDPLR named as future work (p. 15).

method_links.note: First move is an exact QCQP model so that one SDP relaxation exists.
Computation on real benchmarks carries the paper; missing theory stated.
Partial result labelled 'towards'; its own limit proved and set against the computational evidence.
Benchmark filter (older, SDPLR-sized instances) and baseline balance limitation disclosed, but no engineered hard pool.

transferable: Encode 'hyperedge uncut' with a ternary indicator and products y_i(y_i - x_j) = 0 so the objective counts uncut edges exactly (pp. 4-5).
Read the geometry of an SDP's Gram vectors (equal angles to a hub vector, discs) before attempting a rounding analysis (pp. 10-11).
When an analysis falls short, prove where it falls short and report it next to the positive computational evidence (pp. 14-15).

quotes.text: We believe that having a mathematical model is a good starting point for studying the hypergraph minimum-bisection problem.

Although Proposition 4.6 makes sense from a theoretical point of view, it is inconsistent with our computational results in which our method seems to work well on large-scale circuit partitioning problems.

title: Robust rankings for college football
contribution: Measures the sensitivity of Colley Matrix top-25 rankings to switched inconsequential games and proposes CM+, a Γ-budget robust ranking computed from a min-max MINLP by constraint generation, which is empirically much less sensitive.
problem_entry: A 2010 BCS data omission swapped two teams; ask whether Colley rankings (the only fully published BCS computer ranking) are sensitive to games between bottom teams (pp. 4-5, 8).
key_idea: Minimize the worst-case residual ‖Cr - b'‖_2 over Γ switched inconsequential games; C is invariant, b' moves linearly; solve by a convex QP master plus an integer separation subproblem in CPLEX (pp. 12-13).
assumptions: Win/loss data only; robustness only against switches among teams below 30% win rate with top t = 25; deterministic (no stochastic model); omitted games out of scope (pp. 5-6, 8).
proof_devices: invariance C' = C so uncertainty sits only in the right-hand side (p. 12)
Γ ≥ N gives rankings invariant under any switches (p. 16)
experiments: Exhaustive enumeration of all 1- and 2-game switches for 2006-2011; switch measure for CM mean 5.1/max 20 (L = 1) vs CM+ (Γ = 5) mean 1.8/max 10; bubble plots per instance; solves under a minute (pp. 10-11, 14, 18-19).
positioning: Builds on Colley, robust optimization (Bertsimas-Sim style Γ) and robust systems of equations; contrasts with Chartier et al.'s perfect-season stability analysis (pp. 5-6).
writing: Opens with a press quote of the 2010 incident; repeatedly states the chosen definition of robustness and that others are possible (pp. 4-6).
limits_future: No best a priori Γ; larger N, Γ may take hours; rankings hard to compare objectively across Γ; extensions to other sports and other inconsequential sets (pp. 6, 14, 20).

method_links.note: Incumbent stress-tested where it is fragile (all small perturbations of inconsequential games) and the fix judged on the same set; pool rule-based, not filtered for hardness.
Footnote records that the first version used p = ∞ with many alternative optima and credits the referees for the switch to p = 2.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Diagnose the incumbent's sensitivity, then robustify with a budget that nests the incumbent
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Switch-measure histograms for CM first; CM+ reduces to CM at Γ = 0 and is invariant for Γ ≥ N.

transferable: Quantify a base method's fragility by one scalar over all small perturbations and plot base and robust versions on identical scales (pp. 9-11, 18-19).
Solve min-max over a combinatorial uncertainty set by constraint generation: convex master over scenario cuts plus integer separation (p. 13).
Choose the uncertainty budget so Γ = 0 recovers the incumbent and large Γ yields provable invariance (pp. 6, 16).

quotes.text: As far as we are aware, our study is the first explicit attempt to make football rankings robust.
We thank the anonymous referees for suggesting and encouraging a switch to a different p-norm.

title: Newsvendor games: convex optimization of centralized inventory operations
contribution: A closed-form low-rank optimal correlation matrix for the Hartman-Dror SDP that minimizes centralized newsvendor cost, built from a balanced bi- or tri-partition of outlets, and a closed-form nucleolus of the resulting cost game.
problem_entry: Hartman and Dror showed that choosing outlet demand correlations to minimize centralized cost is an SDP; study its structure and a fair (core/nucleolus) allocation (p. 3).
key_idea: The SDP is optimization over the elliptope; Shapiro's theorem classifies cases by sign of v^Tσ; for v^Tσ < 0 solve n = 3 explicitly and lift to any n by a balanced partition, giving rank ≤ 2 (pp. 8-12).
assumptions: Jointly normal demand, identical holding/penalty costs, correlations freely adjustable with fixed means and standard deviations (presented as a perfect-information-style assumption) (pp. 3, 7).
proof_devices: factor R = VV^T with unit rows and σ^T V = 0 (p. 9)
rotation to V_1 = (1,0) for n = 3 uniqueness (pp. 10-11)
aggregation σ^T V* = σ̄^T V̄* = 0 over a balanced partition (Theorem 3.2, p. 12)
rank comparison with Pataki's √(2n) bound (p. 13)
experiments: none (three 6-outlet worked examples on pp. 13-15, not read).
positioning: Extends Eppen and Hartman-Dror; imports Shapiro's minimum-trace-factor-analysis result from statistics; argues nucleolus over Shapley value because the game is not concave (pp. 3, 6-8).
writing: A 'Comments on assumptions' subsection and a managerial-reading subsection that turns the low-rank structure into a grouping rule (pp. 7, 15-16).
limits_future: Normality essential; no fair allocation under general costs; low rank lacks an a priori explanation; constrained correlation changes need a general SDP solver; other distributions open (pp. 7, 15, 17).

method_links.note: Operational question packaged as one convex object (SDP over correlation matrices) and analysed there.
Smallest nontrivial case n = 3 solved exactly, general n reduced to it by aggregation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Closed-form low-rank optimum as structural insight
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Explicit rank-1/2 optimum reveals a grouping rule that a solver's high-rank interior solution would hide.

transferable: Solve the n = 3 case of a structured SDP explicitly, then reduce general n to it via a balanced partition whose aggregated data meet the n = 3 condition (pp. 11-12).
Search for a low-rank optimum through a unit-row factor V with a linear condition σ^T V = 0 (p. 9).
Check adjacent literatures (statistics: minimum-trace factor analysis) for theorems on the same SDP feasible set and credit the pointer (pp. 8, 17).

quotes.text: In this sense, solving (2) via a standard SDP solver does not reveal the structure of Theorem 3.2.
We unfortunately do not have a satisfactory a priori explanation, but it is interesting to understand the implications of this result.
